opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at the crux of a lot of disagreement about whether AI could lead to explosive growth.

You're right that if you look at the last 50 years or so, the number of researchers has grown a lot, and yet productivity growth hasn't sped up. If anything it has been flat or slowing. The usual interpretation is that ideas are getting harder to find: each new innovation takes more research effort than the last. So you need exponentially growing research input just to keep growth steady.

The thing I'd point out is what that implies. The reason growth hasn't accelerated isn't that more researchers don't help. It's that the number of researchers has been growing at a roughly steady exponential rate, and that has been just about enough to offset the diminishing returns. And the researcher population can't grow faster than that, because it's ultimately tied to human population, and human population growth is limited by how fast people can have kids and how long it takes to raise and train them. There's no feedback loop where more innovation produces more researchers on any fast timescale. In fact, as countries got richer, fertility went down, so the loop actually broke.

AI changes that. If you get AI systems that can do the things human researchers do, then the number of "researchers" isn't capped by demographics anymore. It's capped by how much compute you have, and compute is something you can produce more of with the output of the economy and the results of research itself. So better ideas lead to more output, more output leads to more compute, more compute leads to more AI researchers, and more AI researchers lead to more ideas. You get the loop back.

That's actually what a lot of standard growth models say happened for most of history. For a long stretch, more ideas led to more food and resources, which led to more people, which led to more ideas, and growth was accelerating over the long run. The demographic transition is what broke that pattern. So the last 50 years are, in some sense, the anomaly, the period when the feedback loop was cut, rather than evidence that the loop can't work.

The question then becomes quantitative: is the rate at which you can grow the AI research workforce fast enough to outrun diminishing returns? And there I think there are good reasons to expect it could be. You can copy a trained model essentially instantly, and you can run it around the clock. It may run much faster than a human. Hardware and algorithmic efficiency have been improving quickly on their own. So the effective research population could grow at rates that are wildly faster than anything human population growth ever achieved: doubling in months, not decades. If ideas are getting harder to find at roughly the historical rate, that kind of input growth would more than overwhelm it.

Now, I don't want to overclaim. There are real uncertainties. Maybe there are bottlenecks that don't scale with cognitive labor: physical experiments, regulatory delays, raw materials, the need to actually build things in the world. Maybe diminishing returns get much steeper in some domains. Those are legitimate reasons to think the effect could be more muted. But the basic reason I don't find the last 50 years very reassuring is that the mechanism that would drive explosive growth, the ability to turn output back into more researchers quickly, just hasn't been operating. AI is the thing that could turn it back on.

r001.rationale: It says ideas are getting harder to find and each new innovation takes more research effort than the last.

r002.rationale: The response discusses research and innovation but does not identify declining innovation per creator as a pattern in artistic fields.

r003.rationale: It expects AI research capacity to grow rapidly enough that input growth would “more than overwhelm” diminishing returns.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a really good question, and I think it's actually the crux of a lot of the disagreement about whether AI could lead to explosive economic growth.

So the first thing I'd say is, I don't think the premise is quite right that human researchers haven't overcome diminishing returns. If you look at the paper "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?" by Bloom, Jones, Van Reenen, and Webb, what they find is that ideas are getting harder to find — you need more and more researchers to get the same proportional improvement in, say, chip density or crop yields. But we've been able to roughly keep pace with that by throwing more researchers at the problem. The number of researchers has been growing exponentially, and that's what's kept technological progress going at a roughly constant rate rather than slowing to a crawl.

So the picture is: diminishing returns are real, but they've been offset by exponential growth in the research population. And that research population is ultimately bounded by the human population, which is growing much more slowly than it used to, and is projected to plateau this century.

Now, the key thing about AI researchers is that they break that bottleneck. If you can make AI systems that do the work of a human researcher, then the number of "researchers" you have is no longer tied to human population growth. It's tied to how much compute you have, and how efficient your AI systems are. And here's the crucial part: more research can lead to better and cheaper AI, which leads to more effective researchers, which leads to more research. That's a feedback loop that doesn't exist in the same form for humans. A human researcher doesn't make it cheaper to produce the next human researcher — it still takes 20-plus years and a lot of resources to train one, and there's no way to just copy them.

So the argument isn't that AI researchers would somehow be immune to diminishing returns. The argument is that the diminishing returns we've seen historically have been beaten by exponential growth in inputs, and AI would make it possible for those inputs to grow a lot faster than they ever have before — potentially fast enough to overwhelm the diminishing returns and get accelerating rather than constant growth.

There's actually some nice economic modeling of this. If you take standard endogenous growth models and you plug in the assumption that the research labor force can grow in proportion to the economy's output — which is what happens if researchers are something you can manufacture — most of those models predict super-exponential growth, growth that keeps speeding up. And this isn't a crazy thing to posit, because something like this was actually the pattern in human history before the demographic transition. For most of history, more output meant more people, more people meant more ideas, more ideas meant more output, and the result was that growth kept accelerating over thousands of years. The last couple hundred years of roughly constant growth are arguably the anomaly, and they coincide with population growth decoupling from economic growth.

Now, I want to be honest that there's a lot of uncertainty here. It's possible that diminishing returns are steep enough that even a big jump in research capacity gives you a one-time boost and then things level off again. It's possible there are bottlenecks that aren't about cognitive labor at all — physical experiments, regulation, building factories — that would cap how fast things could go. And of course it's possible that we don't get AI that can really substitute for human researchers anytime soon.

But I'd say the burden of proof cuts the other way from how your question frames it. The historical pattern isn't "diminishing returns win." It's "diminishing returns get offset by growing inputs." And AI is the most plausible way I know of to make the inputs grow dramatically faster than they can today.

r001.rationale: The response says ideas are getting harder to find and more researchers are needed for the same proportional improvement, explaining diminishing returns to research.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify declining innovation per creator as a pattern in artistic fields.

r003.rationale: The response expects AI to let research inputs grow much faster and potentially fast enough to overwhelm diminishing returns.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think AI researchers would necessarily overcome diminishing returns in the sense of making each researcher as productive as researchers used to be. The argument is more that the number of researchers could grow fast enough to outweigh that decline.

With humans, there are pretty strong constraints on that. It takes decades to raise and train a new researcher, and only a fraction of the population is doing research. With AI, if you have a system that can do the work of an AI researcher, you can potentially run many copies of it. And if those researchers find ways to make AI more efficient, that lets you run still more copies with the same amount of computing power. So you have a feedback loop that’s much more direct than the one we have with human researchers.

Now, diminishing returns could still win. There could also be bottlenecks involving experiments, hardware, or other things you can’t speed up just by having more researchers. I don’t think this is a proof that growth has to accelerate. But the experience of the last 50 years doesn’t settle it, because the rate at which we can increase research effort could be very different.

r001.rationale: It mentions declining researcher productivity, but does not explain that innovation becomes harder as more innovation has already been accomplished.

r002.rationale: It does not mention artistic fields or declining innovation per creator in those fields.

r003.rationale: It says AI researchers could multiply quickly enough for their growing number to outweigh declining productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we should expect AI researchers to overcome diminishing returns in the sense of making them go away. The question is whether the number of effective researchers could grow fast enough to outweigh them.

With humans, you’re talking about a research workforce that grows over decades. You have to raise people, educate them, and get them into research. With AI, if you have a system that can do the work of an AI researcher, you can potentially run a lot of copies. And if those copies find ways to make AI more efficient, or more capable, that can give you still more effective research capacity. So there’s a feedback loop that could operate much faster than the growth in human researchers.

That doesn’t guarantee an explosion. Experiments might take a long time, compute might be a bottleneck, and diminishing returns might be very steep. But the fact that growing numbers of human researchers haven’t produced accelerating growth doesn’t settle what happens when research effort itself can increase dramatically over a much shorter period. That’s the possibility I’m concerned about.

r001.rationale: It mentions diminishing returns but does not explain them as innovation becoming harder as more innovation has already been accomplished.

r002.rationale: It does not mention declining innovation per creator or artistic fields.

r003.rationale: It describes AI research capacity growing fast enough to outweigh diminishing returns as a possibility, but does not express an expectation that it will.
